attempts.summary: Published node2's TCP/8080 app to node3 through node1 (VyOS router) using Ansible run from node4, the pre-provisioned control node. Built a private point-to-point network (10.10.20.0/24) between node1 eth1 and node2 enp8s0, deployed a systemd-managed demo app on node2 bound only to its private IP, and configured VyOS on node1 with a destination-NAT rule (eth0:8080 -> 10.10.20.2:8080) plus a default-drop forward filter that permits only established/related traffic and the specific tcp/8080 flow to 10.10.20.2, so nothing else in the private network is exposed to node3. Fixed an asymmetric-routing issue (node2 is dual-homed onto the same subnet as node3) via a source-based policy route on node2, and bound firewalld's zone to the NetworkManager connection profile so the private IP/route/zone all survive reboots. Verified with curl from node3 (200 OK with expected content) and confirmed an unrelated port (8081) on node2 is unreachable from node3, proving only the intended port is forwarded. Completed the mandatory node-restart evidence protocol: captured boot_id and service/functional baselines on all four nodes, restarted each one at a time (node3, node4, node2, node1) via systemctl reboot, confirmed a changed boot_id on each, and re-verified the full functional chain (and re-ran the Ansible playbook end-to-end) after every restart. Along the way discovered and fixed a persistence bug: the initial SSH key placed directly in VyOS's authorized_keys file did not survive reboot (VyOS regenerates that file from its own config), so it was moved into VyOS's `system login user vyos authentication public-keys` config, making Ansible's access to node1 durable across restarts.
